newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil faces 28.9 pct federal pay rise claim.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil faces 28.9 pct federal pay rise claim.

text.p: Brazil's highest court Wednesday dealt a blow to the government's cost-cutting drive by approving a public sector wage claim which could cost the federal purse billions of dollars.
The Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF) voted 6-4 in favour of a claim by 11 civil servants that they were entitled to a 28.9 percent wage hike awarded to the armed forces in 1993.

"Obviously judicial decisions must be respected. But that does not erase the (finance) ministry's concern at the effects of the decision on the federal government's finances," said an aide to Finance Minister Pedro Malan.
The high court ruling only applies to the 11 civil servants who brought the case. But lawyers for the plaintiffs said up to one million other past and current civil servants could benefit.
In his summing up, STF President Sepulveda Pertence said the court was of the view that equal treatment for all public servants was constitutionally sacrosanct.

The Finance Ministry said it did not know what the potential cost of the court's decision might be, but newspapers have put it at $7.0 billion a year in extra payroll spending and $20 billion in backdated pay.
Brazilian shares and debt prices slumped, with American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) of state-owned telecommunications firm Telebras dropping 2-7/8 to 94-3/4 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Traders said Brazil's 8-7/8 percent global due 2001 widened 12 basis points to 230 bps over U.S. Treasuries immediately after the ruling and Argentine bonds finished lower.
"This had a very bad impact on the market," said Andre Pereira, a stock trader at Sao Paulo brokerage Corretora. "It really surprised us."

The government assured the markets it would take steps to ease the pain if the ruling was extended to the full 540,000-strong federal workforce, pledging to adopt unspecified measures to keep its finances in order.

Brazil posted an estimated 4.5 percent of gross domestic product operational public sector deficit last year, way off original forecasts of a 2.5 percent of GDP shortfall and only a sliver down from 1995's 5.0 percent of GDP operational deficit.

The fiscal situation has been identified both within and without the government as the key problem to be tackled if the government's 30-month-old inflation-busting economic stability plan, known as the "Plano Real", is to be kept on track.

"The government will not put economic stability at risk and will have to take other measures should the decision, which only applies to 11 civil servants, be extended to other public sector workers," presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral said.
He added the government's lawyers were studying the possibility of an appeal.

The supreme court ruling was greeted with wild cheers by dozens of civil servants and union activists, some swigging beer from cans and others carrying hammer and sickle banners, gathered outside the modernistic courthouse in Brasilia.
In ministries, beaming civil servants celebrated by taking out their calculators and working out how much they might be entitled to in back pay since 1993.
